html:
In March 1835 the government of British India decided to spend its education money on teaching European knowledge in English. The decision followed a famous paper by Thomas Macaulay and shaped the Indian middle class.

Since 1813 the East India Company had set aside a small yearly sum for learning. Officials were split. One side wanted to go on funding Sanskrit and Arabic colleges. The other wanted English. Some Indians did too: Ram Mohan Roy had asked for science teaching in 1823.

Macaulay, the law member of the council, settled it with his Minute of 2 February 1835. He knew no Indian language, and he wrote that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole literature of India and Arabia. The aim, he said, was a class of people Indian in blood and colour but English in taste, opinions and intellect, who would stand between the rulers and the millions they ruled.

English replaced Persian in the higher courts in 1837, and a government job soon required it. The first universities followed in 1857.

The new class did not turn out as planned. Its lawyers, teachers and journalists read Mill and Burke, and founded the Indian National Congress.
sum: In March 1835 the government of British India decided to spend its education money on teaching European knowledge in English. The decision followed a famous paper by Thomas Macaulay and shaped the Indian middle class.
